propositions.text: Claimant is a 50-year-old female citizen of Guyana claiming refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1)(a) and (b).
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX is a 50-year-old female citizen of Guyana, who claims refugee protection pursuant to Sections 96 and 97(1)(a) and (b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1

paragraphs.summary: The claimant is a 50-year-old female citizen of Guyana claiming refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1)(a) and (b).

propositions.text: The panel considered claimant's oral and written testimony, documentary evidence, and counsel's post-hearing submissions in assessing the claim.
propositions.quote: In making the assessment in this claim the panel considered the claimant's oral and written testimony and submissions, documentary evidence entered, before and at the hearing, which included counsel's submissions post hearing.2

paragraphs.summary: The panel considered claimant's testimony, documentary evidence, and counsel's post-hearing submissions in assessing the claim.

propositions.text: Identified issues include exclusion under 1 F(b), identity, credibility, subjective fear, delay in claiming, failure to claim elsewhere, residence in USA, and state protection.
propositions.quote: The issues that were identified at the outset were: Exclusion, 1 F(b); identity; credibility; subjective fear, such as delay in claiming, and failure to claim elsewhere, due to a period of residence in the United States of America (USA) and state protection.

paragraphs.summary: The issues identified include exclusion under 1 F(b), identity, credibility, subjective fear, delay, failure to claim elsewhere, USA residence, and state protection.

propositions.text: Minister raised exclusion issue under Rule 25.
propositions.quote: The issue of Exclusion had been raised by the Minister,3 pursuant to Rule 25.

propositions.text: Claimant detained on arrival at Pearson Airport in 2009 and made claim that day.
propositions.quote: The claimant was detained on XXXX XXXX, 20095 upon arriving at Pearson Airport. She made her claim that day.6

propositions.text: Claimant filed Personal Information Form on Feb 25, 2009, with amendment on May 24, 2011.
propositions.quote: The claimant filed her Personal Information Form (PIF) on February 25, 2009,7 an amendment on May 24, 2011.8

propositions.text: Minister provided Notice of Intent to Intervene on Feb 17 and 18, 2010.
propositions.quote: The Minister provided a Notice of Intent to Intervene on February 17 and 18, 2010.9

paragraphs.summary: Minister raised exclusion under Rule 25; claimant detained on arrival in 2009 and filed PIF with amendment; Minister gave Notice of Intent to Intervene in 2010.

propositions.text: Claimant fears return to Guyana due to domestic abuse by XXXX from 1980-1987, police unhelpful due to connections.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that she fears returning to Guyana because she was the victim of domestic abuse by XXXX XXXX, a man whom she moved in with from 1980 to 1987, XXXX, Guyana. XXXX XXXX told the claimant, who was at that time known as XXXX XXXX, he was a XXXX, and would threaten the claimant with a handgun, if she did not do what he wanted her to do. The claimant went to the police on several occasions for their help, but they did not help her because they were friends with XXXX, her tormentor.

propositions.text: Claimant fled in 1987 to friend's home, met Horriss who sponsored her marriage to USA in 1988.
propositions.quote: In 1987, she ran away to stay at another friends' home in XXXX. While there, she met a man called Horriss who, after learning about her troubles, offered to get her out of Guyana, by sponsoring her in a marriage to him in the USA. In 1988, she married XXXX, and took his last name, XXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant traveled to USA in 1989 as permanent resident, pregnant with child of another man, returned to Guyana to give birth.
propositions.quote: By XXXX 1989, she traveled to the USA and entered the country as a permanent resident10. By this time, she was pregnant with the child of another man she had been dating called XXXX XXXX. Since she had no medical insurance in the USA, she returned to Guyana, to have her baby born there, between XXXX and XXXX 1989.

propositions.text: Claimant left child with mother in Guyana; another boyfriend adopted her older son from earlier man.
propositions.quote: She left the child in the care of her mother, the woman who had raised her, XXXX XXXX. Despite having had another boyfriend, XXXX, adopted her son, who was an older child, from an earlier man.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant alleges fear of return due to domestic abuse and police collusion; fled in 1987, married to enter USA in 1988, returned to Guyana to give birth, left child with mother.

propositions.text: Claimant was charged with grand larceny in 1991 and convicted in spring 1992 for credit card fraud.
propositions.quote: In 1991, the claimant had been charged, with grand larceny, and was convicted in the spring of 1992, due to a matter involving fraudulent credits on credit cards, while working at XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant was charged with grand larceny in 1991 and convicted in 1992 for credit card fraud.

propositions.text: Claimant returned to Guyana in early 1992, got pregnant with third child, born in 1992; partner died in car accident; claimant returned to USA.
propositions.quote: The claimant returned to Guyana in early 1992, to see both of her children. While there, she got pregnant with a third child, from the man she had been dating called XXXX XXXX. The third child was born in XXXX XXXX XXXX 1992, in Guyana. In XXXX 1992, XXXX tragically died in a car accident, in Guyana, and the claimant returned to the USA.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant returned to Guyana in 1992, had third child, partner died in car accident, then returned to USA.

propositions.text: In 1993, claimant saw XXXX at Guyanese restaurant in New York, believes he was in US due to connections.
propositions.quote: In 1993, the claimant saw XXXX XXXX at a Guyanese restaurant in New York, while with two of her children. She believes he was in the US due his connections from being XXXX XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: In 1993, claimant saw XXXX in New York, believes he was in US due to connections.

propositions.text: Claimant returned to Guyana for funeral, was forced by XXXX at gunpoint to his house, stayed few days, then left to Essiquibo for two weeks, then returned to USA.
propositions.quote: The claimant returned to Guyana, to attend a funeral of one of XXXX sons. While at the funeral, she saw XXXX, who forced her to go to his house, by using a gun. She stayed with him, despite his crazed behavior for a few days, and left to go to Essiquibo where she stayed for two weeks. She returned to the USA, after returning to XXXX for a day.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant returned to Guyana for funeral, was forced by XXXX at gunpoint to his house, stayed briefly, then left to Essiquibo, then returned to USA.

propositions.text: After returning to USA, claimant learned her children were taken by XXXX who claimed authority from her.
propositions.quote: After returning the claimant learned that her children had been taken by XXXX, after she left, as XXXX told XXXX, that she had given him authority to take them.

paragraphs.summary: After returning to USA, claimant learned her children were taken by XXXX who claimed authority from her.

propositions.text: In 1995, claimant charged with forgery, sentenced to 1-3 years, supposed to serve 6 months boot camp but did not due to medical issues, completed sentence.
propositions.quote: In 1995, the claimant was charged with forgery while working as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. She was sentenced to 1-3 years in jail, and was supposed to serve 6 months in a boot camp, but due to medical issues, she did not. She completed her sentence.

paragraphs.summary: In 1995, claimant charged with forgery, sentenced to jail, did not serve boot camp due to medical issues, completed sentence.

propositions.text: In 1999, claimant returned to Guyana, lived in hiding in various places, sometimes with friends, sometimes with XXXX by force.
propositions.quote: In 1999, the claimant returned to Guyana. The claimant remained in Guayana, in hiding, living in various places sometimes with friends and other times, with XXXX, by force.

paragraphs.summary: In 1999, claimant returned to Guyana, lived in hiding in various places, sometimes with friends, sometimes with XXXX by force.

propositions.text: In 2004, claimant obtained travel documents under old name, left Guyana to USA via Mexico, found job in Brooklyn.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2004, she obtained travel documents still under the name XXXX XXXX, and departed Guyana, to go to the USA, through Mexico. The claimant obtained a job, and stayed in Brooklyn.

propositions.text: XXXX found claimant in USA, took her back by force, was violent; claimant escaped to Long Island, found work using cousin's identity.
propositions.quote: XXXX, found her in the USA, and took her back with him, again by force, where he was violent towards her. She escaped and went to Port Washington, Long Island, where she found work, in 2005. She was able to find another job, by assuming the identity of XXXX XXXX, her cousin.

paragraphs.summary: In 2004, claimant left Guyana to USA via Mexico, found job; XXXX found and took her back by force; she escaped and worked under cousin's identity.

propositions.text: In 2006, claimant arrested for falsification of documents, incarcerated until 2008, lost US permanent resident status, deported to Guyana in 2008.
propositions.quote: In 2006, the claimant was arrested, and charged with falsification of documents, and she was incarcerated until XXXX 2008. At this time she lost her Permanent Resident Status in the USA, and on XXXX XXXX, 2008, she was deported to Guyana.

paragraphs.summary: In 2006, claimant arrested for document falsification, incarcerated until 2008, lost US permanent resident status, deported to Guyana in 2008.

propositions.text: Upon deportation, claimant detained and confronted by XXXX who knew of her return due to police connection.
propositions.quote: As a result of the deportation, she was detained on arrival, and alleges to have been confronted by XXXX, who knew of her return because of his police connection.

propositions.text: XXXX took claimant by force and held her against her will; she contacted agent who arranged departure in 2009; arrived in Canada in 2009 and was detained for false passport.
propositions.quote: She was taken by force again, by XXXX, and held against her will. While he was away, she was able to contact an agent, who arranged for the claimant's departure, on XXXX XXXX, 2009. She arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, and was told that since her passport was false she would be detained.

paragraphs.summary: Upon deportation, claimant detained and confronted by XXXX; taken by force and held; contacted agent to leave; arrived Canada in 2009 and detained for false passport.

propositions.text: In Canada, claimant learned XXXX is searching for her in Guyana and left messages in Toronto; claimant fears domestic abuse if returned.
propositions.quote: While in Canada, she has learned that XXXX, is searching for her in Guyana, and had left messages for her in Toronto, where she was staying. The claimant believes she would be at risk of domestic abuse by XXXX, her former common-law partner if she returns to Guyana.

paragraphs.summary: In Canada, claimant learned XXXX is searching for her in Guyana and fears domestic abuse if returned.

propositions.text: Accept claimant is citizen of Guyana based on letters and claimant's testimony showing familiarity with Guyana.
propositions.quote: I accept that the claimant is a citizen of Guyana, due to the evidence provided: A letter from the XXXX XXXX XXXX,11 who says she knows XXXX XXXX, "through her sister....whom my sister had a relationship with...and still wants to kill my sister XXXX XXXX.....my family lives in Guyana." Another letter, from XXXX XXXX,12 acknowledges, that she writes for her "Aunt XXXX XXXX" and a letter from XXXX XXXX,13 who writes on behalf of "my daughter XXXX" and finally, a letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX14 who writes, "a man that have my sister XXXX aka XXXX life a miserable hell...a XXXX XXXX in Guyana." The claimant's testimony, showed familiarity with Guyana, and combined with these letters; I accept that the claimant is from that country.

paragraphs.summary: Court accepts claimant is citizen of Guyana based on letters and claimant's testimony.

propositions.text: Claimant arrived with fraudulently obtained passport and birth certificate showing birth in Guyana in 1962.
propositions.quote: The claimant arrived with a passport bearing the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX which it was admitted was fraudulently obtained15 on entry into Canada. She also had in her possession a Birth Certificate,16 indicating her name was XXXX XXXX born in Guyana on XXXX XXXX, 1962.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant arrived with fraudulently obtained passport and birth certificate showing birth in Guyana in 1962.

propositions.text: Claimant admitted criminal history in USA to border official and was detained on entry.
propositions.quote: The claimant admitted that she had a history of criminality in the USA, to the border official, and was detained on entry.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant admitted criminal history in USA to border official and was detained on entry.

propositions.text: Claim was heard June 10, 2011; decision excluded claimant under IRPA Section 98 and Article 1F(b) on July 6, 2011.
propositions.quote: The claim was heard on June 10, 2011, and a decision was made, excluding her on the basis of the operation of Section 98 of the IRPA and Section F(b), of Article 1 of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees ("Article 1F (b)" the claimant on July 6, 2011.

propositions.text: Decision went to judicial review, was overturned April 30, 2012, and returned for rehearing.
propositions.quote: The Reasons for the decision went to Judicial Review, and that decision was overturned on April 30, 2012 and returned to the Board for rehearing.

propositions.text: This decision is from the de novo rehearing.
propositions.quote: This is the decision from the hearing which was heard De Novo.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision excluded claimant under IRPA Section 98 and Article 1F(b); judicial review overturned it and returned for rehearing; this is the de novo decision.

propositions.text: Exclusion clause 1 F(b) applies to the claimant due to serious reasons for considering she committed a serious non-political crime before refugee admission.
propositions.quote: I find that the exclusion clause 1 F(b) is applicable to the claimant as I find that there are serious reasons for considering that the claimant has committed a serious non-political crime outside the country of refuge prior to her admission to that country as a refugee.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds exclusion clause 1 F(b) applies to the claimant for serious non-political crimes before refugee admission.

propositions.text: Section 98 IRPA excludes persons under Article 1(E) or (F) of the UN Refugee Convention from protected person status.
propositions.quote: Section 98 of the IRPA17 indicates that persons to whom Article 1(E) or (F) of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees applies are not considered to be protected persons.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Section 98 IRPA excludes persons under Article 1(E) or (F) of the UN Refugee Convention from protection.

propositions.text: Article 1(F)(b) excludes persons with serious reasons for considering they committed serious non-political crimes before refugee admission.
propositions.quote: Article 1(F). The provisions of this Convention shall not apply to any person with respect to whom there are serious reasons for considering that: (b) he has committed a serious non-political crime outside the country of refuge prior to his admission to that country as a refugee.

paragraphs.summary: The court quotes Article 1(F)(b) excluding persons with serious reasons for serious non-political crimes before refugee admission.

propositions.text: The Minister reproduced the basis of intervention and relevant rules, law and elements for intervention in documents.
propositions.quote: The Minister has reproduced the basis of intervention and the relevant rules, law and elements required for intervention which are referred to in the documents.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister reproduced the basis and relevant rules for intervention in documents.

propositions.text: The Minister argues the claimant should be excluded from protection due to her criminal history in the USA.
propositions.quote: The Minister's position is that the claimant should be excluded from protection under the Convention because of her criminal history in the USA.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister argues the claimant should be excluded due to her USA criminal history.

propositions.text: Jayasekara sets criteria for interpreting exclusion clause Article 1F(b) regarding crime seriousness, including crime elements, prosecution mode, penalty, facts, and circumstances.
propositions.quote: In Jayasekara the Federal Court of Appeal20 determined criteria for the interpretation of the exclusion clause in Article 1F(b), as regards the seriousness of a crime. It requires an evaluation of the elements of the crime, the mode of prosecution, the penalty prescribed, the facts, and the mitigating and aggravating circumstances underlying the conviction.

propositions.text: A presumption that a crime is serious may be rebutted by assessing factors like hybrid offences and prosecution mode differences.
propositions.quote: A presumption that a crime is serious may be rebutted by the assessment of those factors and it is important to be mindful of the hybrid nature offences in Canada and the other country and the relevance of the choice in the mode of prosecution and if there was a substantial difference between the penalty prescribed for a summary conviction offence and that for an indictable offence.

propositions.text: The claimant has three convictions for grand larceny, forgery, and falsifying business records with Canadian equivalents and sentences described.
propositions.quote: Summary of the Claimant's Convictions 1. A conviction of grand larceny, in the 3rd degree, class D felony, PL 155.35, arrested XXXX XXXX XXXX 1991, convicted XXXX XXXX 1992 on a plea of guilty and sentenced to 5 years probation, which was discharged XXXX XXXX XXXX, 1997 due to her incarceration for the conviction in 1996 below;21The Canadian Criminal equivalent, is one of Offences Against rights of Property, in the section entitled Theft, 322 (1); 330 (1) Theft by a person required to account; or under Offences resembling Theft such as 342 (Theft, forgery etc. of credit card). The maximum punishment for the first two offenses, provide for a punishment for a tem not exceeding ten years at s. 334 (a) which is the same for the third 342 (1) (e). 2. A conviction of grand larceny arrested in XXXX 1995, 3rd degree, class D felony, PL 155.35, forgery, 2nd degree, Class D felony PL 170.10. In this case she was convicted in XXXX 1996, after a plea of guilty to attempted grand larceny, Class E Felony, PL 110/155.35 and sentenced to 18 month to 3 years and some restitution and after being admitted to a Correctional Facility in XXXX 1996 she was released in XXXX 1997, and paroled to US Immigration; The Canadian equivalent for this crime most closely resembles Forgery described in s. 366 (1) in that the claimant made a false document, knowing it to be false, such as the cheques of the XXXX XXXX she worked for, and with the intent that it should be used as genuine, to the prejudice of the XXXX, who was supposedly her friend. In this case, the punishment described at s. 367 involves a term of up to 14 years. 3. A conviction after being arrested XXXX XXXX XXXX 2006 for possession of a forged instrument, class D felony, PL 170.25 forgery, 2nd degree; deed, will co, Class D felony PL 170.10, falsifying business records, 1st degree, class E Felony, PL 175.10, and she was convicted XXXX XXXX XXXX 2006 on a plea of guilty to falsify business records, 1st degree, Class E felony, PL 175.10 and sentenced to a range between 18 months and 3 years and some restitution, and the claimant was admitted to the same facility as before in XXXX 2007 until XXXX 2008 and paroled to US Immigration.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Jayasekara criteria for crime seriousness and summarizes claimant's three convictions with Canadian equivalents and sentences.

propositions.text: Claimant's criminal history was confirmed by RCMP fingerprint comparison matching her identity on entry to Canada in 2009.
propositions.quote: It is noted that the criminal history of the claimant was determined, through an R.C.M.P. fingerprint comparison, which were found to be identical to XXXX XXXX, born XXXX XXXX, 1962, and taken from the claimant's fingerprints, on entry to Canada XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's criminal history was confirmed by RCMP fingerprint comparison on entry to Canada in 2009.

propositions.text: The claimant admits convictions but claims mitigating circumstances should be considered.
propositions.quote: The claimant admitted that she was convicted of the crimes in the USA but claimed that there were mitigating circumstances that underlie these events which have to be considered.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant admits convictions but claims mitigating circumstances should be considered.

propositions.text: Completion of sentence does not preclude exclusion; 'serious reasons for considering' is a lower standard than 'balance of probabilities'.
propositions.quote: Referring to the section of the law concerned, and the jurisprudence, the panel notes that the fact that the claimant completed her sentence doesn't mean that that she cannot be excluded for the crime. It is also noted that the claimant need not have been charged or convicted of a crime, as the clause in question, refers to "committing" a crime. The standard of proof is "serious reasons for considering" which is less than a "balance of probabilities."

paragraphs.summary: The panel notes sentence completion doesn't preclude exclusion; standard is 'serious reasons for considering', lower than balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Panel can consider Canadian law's view of the offence seriousness; Minister provided certificates of disposition and offence details.
propositions.quote: In evaluating the seriousness of the crimes, the panel can refer to the view which Canadian law takes of that offence. The Minister has provided documentary evidence, which included the certificates of Disposition as well as printout details of the offences in question.

paragraphs.summary: The panel can consider Canadian law's view; Minister provided certificates of disposition and offence details.

propositions.text: Minister argues first offence (1991 grand larceny) is not serious as Canadian equivalent would not generate a 10 year sentence due to amount under $3000.
propositions.quote: Referring to the first (1.) offence noted above, grand larceny, which was from an arrest in 1991, and conviction in 1992, the Minister's position is that to be serious the Canadian offense would not have generated a 10 year sentence, as the amount in question was determined to be under $3000. As a result, that particular offense should not be considered "serious"

paragraphs.summary: The Minister argues the first offence is not serious due to low amount and Canadian sentencing.

propositions.text: Claimant worked for an agency 1992-1995 and admitted living under another name and enduring abuse, giving money to husband to keep peace.
propositions.quote: Regarding the second (2.) Offense; The claimant worked as a XXXX XXXX for an agency in Long Island New York from 1992 to 1995. She worked for XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The claimant was supposed to be helping her. On questioning by the Minister and her counsel about the circumstances surrounding the charges the claimant admitted that she lived in the USA as XXXX XXXX, not as XXXX XXXX, and that she had to endure living with XXXX XXXX, as she was married to him, that she had to give him all her money, a way of keeping peace with him.

propositions.text: Claimant explained using cheques from a friend to 'run away' and did not recall telling judge about reasons for actions.
propositions.quote: She explains in her PIF28, that XXXX XXXX XXXX was a friend of hers and she used to give her checks, and she was asked what she did with the cheques from XXXX XXXX XXXX? She said the XXXX was involved, and that she remembered putting two cheques in the bank. She said she did these things "to run away". She was asked if she told the judge about why she did these things, and she did not recall what the judge said.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant admits living under another name, enduring abuse, using cheques to 'run away', and not recalling telling the judge.

propositions.text: Claimant stated low self-esteem and suicidal thoughts during two offences; dismissed counseling and had legal counsel but unclear if judge heard reasons.
propositions.quote: Regarding the two other offenses, arrest in XXXX 1995, convicted in 1996, for which she served time for a year; and then the second offense which occurred 10 years later, for which she served an another year, the claimant stated that she was not thinking straight, that her self-esteem was very low, and that she "wanted to run away and kill herself." She was asked if during the court process she had the opportunity to tell the court about why she committed the crimes. She said she was speaking to a counselor, who was of no help, and that they sent her to classes. She said her mind was not clear. The panel finds that the claimant admits that she was offered assistance, but dismissed it, because of her state of mind. In reviewing the notes the panel also notes that the claimant did state that this counseling and the classes was for the previous matter, and the claimant doesn't recall what the judge said to her when she explained why she committed the crimes. The claimant had counsel, and despite her state of mind she represented by legal counsel and had an opportunity to state her case.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant stated low self-esteem and suicidal thoughts, dismissed counseling, had legal counsel, but unclear if judge heard reasons.

propositions.text: Minister presented media evidence identifying claimant swindling $15,000; claimant pled guilty and had opportunity to state case.
propositions.quote: The Minister presented evidence that the claimant was identified by the media, as having swindled an XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX of $15,000, which was the amount of restitution was $15,000 29 and the claimant stated that XXXX XXXX XXXX was a friend, and yet she put XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXs name on blank checks to the XXXX. The claimant pled guilty to this offense, according to the court records, as she clearly had had an opportunity to state her case.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister presented media evidence of claimant swindling $15,000; claimant pled guilty and had opportunity to state case.

propositions.text: Claimant said she was pressured and had no one to trust, thinking of children, but stole from employer anyway.
propositions.quote: She was asked during the hearing about the lesser matter in 1992 when she worked at XXXX. In that case she said that she was "being pressured" and that she was trying to get away. She said she had "no where to turn no one I could trust, and I was thinking of my children...." She was asked what she did with the money, and her immediate response was, "I don't know."

propositions.text: Panel observed claimant candid but self-esteem low; crime not serious but claimant used false name contrary to identity documents.
propositions.quote: The panel observed the claimant, and though she was candid about what she did, the added element, "my self-esteem was low" is an evaluation that the claimant has made on her own, of herself. The panel's observation, that the claimant needed money, probably did think of her children, but then proceeded to steal from the place where she was employed, anyway. She does not seem to be aware, or possibly pretended not to be present to the crime of theft. That the money was not in cash, it was a credit card, that she was being pressured by some others. This crime in itself was not serious, according to the criteria, however, the panel notes, she was XXXX XXXX, at the time, which she is now saying is not her real name, which is contrary to identity documents such as the Birth Certificate she has provided.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant said she was pressured and thinking of children but stole; panel found crime not serious but claimant used false name.

propositions.text: No requirement to consider good character; claimant was good for 10 years but reoffended using false identity to work.
propositions.quote: The panel notes that there is no requirement, to consider a claimant's "good character" despite the passage of time, in this particular case the claimant might have been "good" for ten years, but then was arrested and convicted again while working at XXXX XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant used another identity knowing she could not get a job as herself due to criminal record.
propositions.quote: The claimant in this case, was using another identity, XXXX XXXX, knowing she could not get a job, as XXXX XXXX, because of her criminal record.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds no good character consideration; claimant reoffended using false identity to work.

propositions.text: Claimant knew using another name was illegal but did it anyway; panel drew negative inferences and found claimant not credible.
propositions.quote: The panel drew a negative inference, from her reply that she was not thinking straight at the time. The panel found that she was aware it was illegal to use another person's identity, but she did it anyway. The panel drew a negative inference as to the fact that she would again present herself as someone else so as to work in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, despite having been charged and convicted for forging cheques of an XXXX XXXX, in the ten years before. It shows that she is intending to act falsely; she is pretending to be someone else, obtaining a driver's license in someone else's name to document her identity so that she can work again, for XXXX XXXX. The panel drew a negative inference for her attempt to conceal her identity. The panel finds that she is very resourceful, with a consistent intention to act falsely. As a result, the panel did not trust her and found her to be not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The panel found claimant knew using another name was illegal, drew negative inferences, and found her not credible.

propositions.text: Claimant said third conviction was while using cousin's identity to work and trying to escape ex-abuser, causing strong physical reaction.
propositions.quote: She was also asked about her third conviction by her counsel and she stated that it was while she was using her cousin's identity to work in Long Island. At the time, she stated that she was trying to get away, from her ex-abuser XXXX, whom she had seen in New York at around that time, at a restaurant. This reply caused the claimant to have a strong physical reaction in the hearing room.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant said third conviction was while using cousin's identity to work and escaping ex-abuser, causing strong reaction.

propositions.text: Panel did not find claimant credible and found no mitigating factors to minimize crime seriousness.
propositions.quote: Overall the panel did not find the claimant credible, and the panel did not find that there were mitigating factors that would minimize the seriousness of the crimes.

paragraphs.summary: The panel did not find claimant credible and found no mitigating factors to minimize crime seriousness.

propositions.text: Minister provided aggravating circumstances including claimant admitting crime but blaming another person and media coverage of $15,000 cheque forgery.
propositions.quote: The Minister has provided aggravating circumstances for the underlying convictions. For example the 1996 conviction for attempted grand larceny concerned XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, whom the claimant referred to as a friend "who used to give me cheques as gifts".31 She also adds that "The XXXX took some blank cheques from XXXX XXXX XXXX. I also signed XXXX XXXX XXXX name on some cheques and put those into my account." The claimant is admitting the crime and yet blaming another person, the XXXX. The Minister suggests that the claimant is attempting to minimize the gravity, that there was someone else involved. The Minister showed that there was news coverage of the crime in the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX,32 regarding this particular crime, showing that the claimant, then known as XXXX XXXX, was convicted of forging $15,000 in cheques drawn on the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX account. The panel notes that the claimant is very confused, and troubled. In the PIF she claims XXXX XXXX XXXX is a friend, while signing cheques with her name and depositing it to her account on behalf of the XXXX. The panel just doesn't believe the claimant about her role in this matter as being a friend to XXXX XXXX XXXX. The panel finds that the court record, the media reports, all show a consistent story, which is incongruent with the claimant's testimony.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister provided aggravating circumstances including claimant admitting crime but blaming another and media coverage of $15,000 forgery; panel disbelieves claimant.

propositions.text: The third conviction in 2006 was for falsifying business records in the USA, possibly under section 368 or s. 403 Personation.
propositions.quote: The third conviction, in 2006, refers to an offence of falsifying business records in the USA. Which could be considered section 368 "uttering forged document" which is a hybrid offence that carries a maximum term of 10 years imprisonment if prosecuted by way of indictment or s. 403, Personation.

propositions.text: The claimant secured employment by assuming her cousin's identity and was deported to Guyana as a result.
propositions.quote: The claimant secured employment at another XXXX XXXX, by way of assuming another person's identity, her cousin. As a result of this offense she was deported back to Guyana.

propositions.text: The claimant said she assumed another's identity because she could not get a job as herself.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked why she did that; she replied because she could not get a job as XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant's 2006 conviction involved falsifying records and identity assumption, leading to deportation because she couldn't get a job as herself.

propositions.text: The claimant said she did not realize her true name until many years later and feared her criminal past and abuser.
propositions.quote: She also stated that she did not realize her true name until many years later. She was asked why she thought she could not get a job as XXXX XXXX, and she said because of her criminal past, and because my abuser XXXX was getting away with things.

propositions.text: The claimant admitted knowing it was illegal to use a different name but said she wasn't thinking right.
propositions.quote: Did you know it was illegal to use a different name? Her reply, "yes but I wasn't thinking right."

propositions.text: The panel empathizes with the claimant but notes a pattern of theft and deception from 1991-2006, including working under false pretenses.
propositions.quote: The panel feels empathy for the claimant who no doubt was trying to make a living, however, she kept going back to the past behaviors, working for XXXX whom she had stolen from, and she had stolen from XXXX, a previous employer, and continuing to work for the XXXX while pretending to be someone else. This pattern extends from 1991-2006, after serving two terms in a maximum security facility, one of which could have been in Canada, for a maximum term of 14 years.

propositions.text: These elements point to serious reasons to exclude the claimant for non-political crime.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that all these elements point to serious reasons to exclude the claimant. Non-political Crime

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the claimant's admission of illegal identity use, empathizes but finds a pattern of theft and deception justifying exclusion for non-political crime.

propositions.text: The crimes were non-political as the claimant sought money, not political motives or disturbance.
propositions.quote: The crimes are non-political as the claimant wanted money. There was no political motive, no political disturbance related to any struggle to modify or abolish a government policy or a government.

propositions.text: The claimant said she was running away or trying to keep peace with her husband by giving him money.
propositions.quote: The claimant stated that she was running away, or trying to keep the peace with her husband so had to give him money.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's crimes were non-political, motivated by money and personal reasons, not political struggle.

propositions.text: The crimes charged in the USA are non-political crimes.
propositions.quote: As a result the crimes that the claimant was charged with in the USA are non-political crimes.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the claimant's USA crimes are non-political.

propositions.text: The claimant was tried in the USA under democratic legal rules and had counsel, responding about her lawyer and courses.
propositions.quote: The claimant was tried in the United States of America, and was prosecuted according to rules of law that are considered democratic, and she had counsel, as she clearly responded to questions about what she told her lawyer, and the counselor, and courses she was given, that she said were not useful.

propositions.text: The Minister provided background on mitigating factors of the crimes and claimant.
propositions.quote: The Minister provided background information on the mitigating factors of the crimes as well as the claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the claimant was fairly tried in the USA and the Minister provided mitigating background information.

propositions.text: The claimant provided a medical report showing Battered Women Syndrome, PTSD, and Dissociative Identity Disorder.
propositions.quote: The claimant provided documents such as a medical report,33 showing that the claimant suffered from Battered Women Syndrome, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, and Dissociative Identity Disorder.

propositions.text: It was argued the claimant should be treated as a Vulnerable Person and circumstances considered in her protection claim.
propositions.quote: As a result of that report it was argued that the claimant should be treated as a Vulnerable Person, and that the underlying circumstances should be considered in light of her claim for protection.

propositions.text: This was allowed in the original hearing but not dealt with in the present hearing; Gender guidelines were considered.
propositions.quote: This was allowed, in the original hearing, however it was not dealt with in the present hearing. The Gender guidelines34, were considered.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant submitted medical evidence of trauma and argued vulnerability, allowed previously but not addressed here; Gender guidelines considered.

propositions.text: The claimant provided identity documents consistently identifying her as XXXX XXXX and later XXXX.
propositions.quote: The claimant, provided identity documents such as a Birth Certificate, for XXXX XXXX35 which it was noted did not have seal, as well as a marriage certificate, and Divorce Certificate in Ontario, for XXXX XXXX XXXX, made here in Ontario, and dated XXXX XXXX, 2010,36 which is consistent with a Marriage Certificate also provided 37 and a copy of passport38 from Guyana, all of which identify the claimant consistently, as XXXX XXXX, and later XXXX.

propositions.text: The court believes the claimant has no other identity and accepts her identity as XXXX XXXX based on fingerprints and documents.
propositions.quote: I do not believe that the claimant, has another identity, and I have treated the claimant as XXXX XXXX, as her fingerprints are consistent with that identity, which I accept as valid, as well as the above documents.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant provided consistent identity documents; the court accepts her identity as XXXX XXXX based on fingerprints and documents.

propositions.text: The claimant arrived on a fraudulent passport and claims her real name is XXXX XXXX, given by her biological mother to another person.
propositions.quote: Notwithstanding these documents, this claimant, who arrived on a fraudulent passport, is now claiming that her real name is XXXX XXXX as she asserts her real biological mother "gave" her to XXXX XXXX many years ago.

propositions.text: No valid document supports the claimant's claim of another identity.
propositions.quote: There is no valid document to support this.

propositions.text: The panel referred to a medical opinion noting possible multiple personalities explaining incongruent behaviors and memory problems.
propositions.quote: The panel, referred to the medical opinion39 which states: "I have not yet followed her long enough to identify discrete multiple personalities, but given her extremely traumatic history, the presence of these is not unlikely and could explain her incongruent behaviors. It could explain why she would have committed credit card theft and forging cheques without having been able to appreciate that her actions were illegal....she is having trouble problems with memory and concentration."

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the claimant's fraudulent passport and unsubstantiated identity claim, referencing a medical opinion on possible multiple personalities.

propositions.text: The medical opinion confirms the panel observed incongruent behavior inconsistent with facts and Minister's documents.
propositions.quote: The medical opinion confirms what the panel observed throughout the hearing, "incongruent behaviour".

propositions.text: The claimant minimized involvement and continued a 15-year pattern including entering Canada with a fraudulent passport and false identity.
propositions.quote: The claimant attempted to minimize her involvement, and continues to act in ways that continue her history, which now extends over a 15-year period of time, such as entering Canada with a fraudulent passport, and purporting to be a different person, with a different name and birth certificate.

propositions.text: The claimant has convictions for theft, forgery, and personation and pretends to be someone else with inconsistent evidence.
propositions.quote: The claimant has been convicted of theft, forgery, and personation. For the claim, she is pretending that she now really someone else, and has one birth certificate, and some personal letters as evidence, frankly, the panel is not persuaded.

propositions.text: The panel sees the claimant as living a life of false pretenses, including entering Canada with a false passport.
propositions.quote: The panel sees a woman who has made a life of false pretenses, by words and actions; even entering Canada, with a false passport.

propositions.text: The panel does not believe the claimant's emotional displays prove serious illness beyond intent to deceive.
propositions.quote: The panel does not believe the sincerity of the pauses, the tears, the drifts during sentences, as evidence that she is suffering from anything more serious than an intent to deceive.

propositions.text: The medical opinion confirms the panel's view that incongruence is more about intent to deceive than trauma.
propositions.quote: The medical opinion, confirms what I observed. To me the inconguence, had less to do with having been battered, or abandoned, but more to do, with having an intention to represent a condition, in order to persuade that it is a fact. I am not persuaded.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's behavior incongruent, minimizing crimes, living false pretenses, and doubts sincerity of claimed trauma or illness.

propositions.text: The Minister has met the burden to show the claimant committed serious non-political crimes outside Canada before admission.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that the Minister has met the burden of showing that the claimant has committed serious non-political crimes outside Canada, prior to her admission.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Minister proved the claimant committed serious non-political crimes before admission.

propositions.text: The Minister's counsel has the burden to prove the claimant should be excluded from protection.
propositions.quote: The Minister's counsel has the burden of proving that the claimant should be excluded from protection.

propositions.text: The IRPA standard is 'serious reasons for considering', requiring more than suspicion but less than balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The standard of proof required by the IRPA is that there be "serious reasons for considering".40 In Mugesera, the Supreme Court held that this standard requires something more than suspicion or conjecture, but something less than proof on a balance of probabilities.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister bears the burden to prove exclusion with a standard of 'serious reasons for considering' per IRPA and Mugesera.

propositions.text: The crimes under consideration are serious non-political crimes.
propositions.quote: In the present case, the excludable crimes under consideration are serious non-political crimes.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the crimes considered are serious non-political crimes.

propositions.text: In Chan, a serious non-political crime is equated with one punishable by 10+ years imprisonment in Canada.
propositions.quote: In Chan 43 the court stated that "had the appellant engaged in similar conduct in Canada, he would have been convicted of an offence such as drug trafficking for which a maximum prison term of ten years or more could have been imposed. In other words, for present purposes I will presume, without deciding, that a serious non political crime is to be equated with one in which a maximum sentence of ten years or more could have been imposed had the crime been committed in Canada."

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Chan equating serious non-political crime with offenses punishable by 10+ years in Canada.

propositions.text: The claimant's vague explanations for convictions show a pattern of thief and con-woman; the court did not believe her.
propositions.quote: I find that the claimant's explanations for her vagueness on the first charge in 1991, and then the second conviction in 1996, followed by the third in 2006, show a pattern of behavior of a thief, and a con-woman. I didn't believe her.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's vague explanations reveal a pattern of theft and deception and does not believe her.

propositions.text: There are serious reasons to consider the claimant convicted of serious non-political crimes and excluded under Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention.
propositions.quote: I find that there are serious reasons for considering that the claimant was convicted of crimes of a serious non-political nature and, thus, is a person referred to in Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention.

propositions.text: The Refugee Protection Division excludes the claimant from refugee protection and rejects her claim.
propositions.quote: Thus, the Refugee Protection Division determines that the claimant is excluded from the refugee protection afforded Convention refugees and persons in need of protection and, accordingly, rejects her claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the claimant is excluded from refugee protection under Article 1F(b) and rejects her claim.

propositions.text: The panel finds the claimant is excluded from protection and signs the decision dated March 12, 2013.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that the claimant is excluded from protection. (signed) "Me Dominique Setton" Me Dominique Setton March 12, 2013 Date

paragraphs.summary: The panel formally finds the claimant excluded from protection and signs the decision on March 12, 2013.
